strengths: Well-motivated application domain: Fire reconstruction from sparse views is a challenging and underexplored problem with practical relevance.
Complete technical pipeline addressing coupled challenges: temporal synchronization, rolling shutter distortion, sparse-view geometry, and high-frequency dynamics are integrated systematically.
Real-world dataset with diverse fuel types: Evaluation on actual fire captures (not synthetic) with varying combustion conditions demonstrates practical grounding.
Comprehensive ablation studies: Table 2 provides clear analysis of component contributions (sync, rolling shutter, flow init, static/dynamic separation).
Practical hardware contribution: LED-based microsecond-level synchronization achieves sub-frame precision with commodity equipment, addressing a real deployment challenge.
Clear presentation and visualization: Generally well-written with effective pipeline visualizations and novel-view renderings that clearly convey the approach.
Sensible depth initialization strategy: Combining stereo with monocular regularization is a reasonable approach for sparse-view under-constrained optimization.
weaknesses: Fundamentally unfair baseline comparisons: 4DGS methods [92, 104] were designed for dense multi-view capture; comparing them with random initialization on 3-view data with GPU memory caps (10^6 Gaussians) disadvantages them. No comparison with physics-informed fire methods [15, 28] that are directly relevant.

Critically small and poorly-split dataset: 17 sequences × 100 frames (~1,700 frames total) is insufficient to establish a benchmark or demonstrate generalization. Train/test split uses every 8th frame within sequences, risking overfitting to specific fire instances rather than held-out sequences.

Inconsistent baseline performance interpretation: 4DGS (Yang et al.) achieves higher full-frame PSNR/SSIM (35.29/0.9623 vs 33.61/0.9504), indicating better background quality, but worse depth metrics. The proposed method prevents background dynamics to maintain geometric consistency—unclear which is 'better,' yet claimed as superiority.

Limited methodological novelty: The approach primarily combines existing techniques (3DGS, FreeTimeGS [88], MEMFOF, standard depth estimation). Individual novel components are incremental: flow-based initialization is straightforward projection; rolling shutter handling applies known linear approximations (minimal impact: Table 2, 27.48 vs 27.46); static/dynamic separation is standard practice.

Questionable core design choices: (1) Minimum intensity projection for fire removal assumes fire is always brightest—fragile for reflective surfaces or emissive backgrounds. (2) Linear velocity model acknowledged to oversmooth turbulent motion but not validated or improved. (3) Depth ground-truth against monocular estimates is circular; both may be equally inaccurate for transparent/emissive fire.

Inappropriate metrics for semi-transparent emissive phenomena: PSNR/SSIM are poor proxies for fire quality. Only LPIPS reported for perceptual metrics. No temporal coherence metrics, motion trajectory validation, or user studies. Flame realism and high-frequency fidelity difficult to assess from pixel-wise scores.

Ablation results undermine claimed contributions: Rolling shutter removal has negligible impact (27.48 vs 27.46 PSNRflame). Synchronization removal with 1-frame offset causes only mild degradation (27.12 vs 27.46), suggesting these prominently-featured components are not critical to reported performance.

Weak robustness analysis for stated limitations: Paper acknowledges dense optical flow fails in high-emission and low-texture regions (ubiquitous in fire) but provides no mitigation, sensitivity analysis, or robustness validation. No evaluation of performance degradation with optical flow quality, synchronization jitter, or sub-3-view scenarios.

Incomplete reproducibility: Code and full dataset promised but not provided for review. Many hyperparameters lack justification (lifetime = 4× frame time, α₀ values, learning rate choices). Custom hardware synchronization is difficult to replicate outside specialized labs.

Missing analysis and comparisons: No comparison with simpler baselines or physics-informed methods. No temporal coherence/optical flow consistency metrics. No failure case analysis. No computational cost comparison. No user studies for perceptual validation of flame realism.

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: fire reconstruction from sparse (3) views addresses a genuinely challenging and under-explored application
Technically sound pipeline: The two-stage static/dynamic separation is well-justified; flow-based initialization and FreeTimeGS representation are appropriate design choices
Novel hardware contribution: LED-based sub-frame synchronization exploiting rolling shutter to achieve microsecond-level precision is creative engineering
Comprehensive experimental validation: 17 diverse real-world sequences with thorough ablations (rolling shutter, synchronization, flow initialization, static/dynamic separation)
Geometric consistency: Unlike baselines, maintains spatially plausible depth (RMSEdepth=0.041 vs 0.27 for 4DGS methods), valuable for applications beyond rendering
Strong flame-specific performance: Significantly outperforms baselines on PSNRflame and SSIMflame with low variance across scenes
Reproducibility-focused: Code and dataset promised; detailed implementation descriptions; custom hardware design documented
Clear presentation: Well-written pipeline description, effective visualizations, honest limitations discussion that strengthens credibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Primarily combines existing components (3DGS, FreeTimeGS, optical flow, depth priors); static/dynamic decomposition is standard; core innovation is engineering rather than fundamental algorithm design

Narrow baseline comparisons: Only compares against two 4DGS variants; missing comparisons with Dynamic 3D Gaussians, ODE-GS, MoSca, and NeRF-based methods. Baselines appear fundamentally unsuited for sparse views, making it unclear how much improvement is method-specific vs. problem-formulation mismatch

Limited dataset scope: Only 17 sequences (~100 frames each); all fires visually similar (propane, wood, cardboard, paper); controlled indoor settings; no smoke-heavy, large outdoor, or extreme-condition scenarios; single camera model/frame rate
Indirect depth validation: No ground truth available for semi-transparent emissive fire; evaluation against monocular depth estimates is indirect and potentially unreliable for transparent regions

Critical technical details missing/underjustified: Tikhonov regularization α0 never specified; voxel size unspecified; Gaussian lifetime (4× frame time) lacks justification; depth loss weight factor of 100 never ablated; random voxel offset range not analyzed

Optical flow dependency under-analyzed: Despite claims about flow importance, RandFlow ablation shows only 0.45 PSNR drop; inconsistency suggests either flow is less critical than claimed or metric is insensitive; no flow error propagation analysis

Rolling shutter handling questionable: Linear approximations assume ∇t·v≈11·10⁻³ is 'small' (~1%), but GlobalShutter ablation shows only +0.02 improvement; suggests time/effort allocation may be disproportionate

Evaluation metrics limited: PSNR/SSIM poorly suited for transparent/emissive materials; LPIPS is general perceptual metric; no user studies or domain expert evaluation; no metrics directly measuring motion field quality

Weak ablation evidence for synchronization: NoSync shows only 0.34 PSNR drop (27.46→27.12); does not justify elaborate hardware requirement; limits adoption and reproducibility for users without custom ESP32 setup
Generalization concerns: No robustness tests for calibration errors; no graceful degradation with <3 views; no experiments on non-fire emissive phenomena; tuned for specific fire appearance

Incomplete baseline analysis: Figure 9 shows baselines producing spatial degeneracies, but unclear if this reflects method superiority or sparse-view unsuitability; missing comparisons with baselines using denser views
Missing experiments: No failure case analysis; no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; no optical flow method comparisons; no performance evaluation on other emissive phenomena

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Identifies specific failure modes of existing dynamic GS methods when applied to fire (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift) with compelling justification for why fire violates fundamental assumptions of persistent-primitive methods

Technically sound methodology combining stereo-monocular depth fusion for static background with flow-based initialization and explicit temporal parameterization (lifetime, velocity) appropriate for transient phenomena

Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation including frame-wise metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), depth consistency (RMSEdepth), novel density-weighted volumetric evaluation (DVE) protocol for motion assessment, and thorough ablation studies
Practical systems contribution: ESP32-based LED synchronization achieving ~15 µs sub-frame precision with rolling shutter exploitation makes high-speed fire capture feasible with commodity hardware
Real-world dataset of 17 fire sequences at 400 Hz with three synchronized views and diverse fuel types (propane, wood, gasoline, cardboard, paper) will benefit future research
Convincing qualitative results with clear visual superiority over baselines; rendered depth maps demonstrate both visual and geometric improvements over 4DGS, Grid4D, and FreeTimeGS
Clear presentation with well-articulated motivation and detailed methodology; thorough supplementary material with implementation details, pipeline visualizations, and per-scene results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components (static/dynamic separation, flow-based initialization, constant-velocity model) are relatively straightforward; primary contribution is in combination and application rather than fundamental methodological innovation

Highly restrictive experimental scope: Only 3-camera setup tested; no exploration of 2-view, 4+ view, or truly monocular scenarios; all experiments in controlled lab environment with fixed camera configuration; method requires custom hardware synchronization

Baseline comparison limitations: Restricts quantitative comparison to GS methods only, excluding physics-informed methods (e.g., [15, 29, 36]) and NeRF-based approaches that might offer better accuracy despite higher computational cost; FreeTimeGS comparison uses unfair initialization (RoMa with failures shown in Fig. 12) while other baselines use COLMAP

Fundamental methodological robustness concerns: Heavy reliance on optical flow which fails in emissive low-texture regions; linear velocity model acknowledged as insufficient for turbulent flames; alpha loss creates visual-physical accuracy trade-off (NoMask ablation shows higher visual metrics but degraded motion fidelity); ablations show simultaneous static-dynamic optimization significantly degrades full-image metrics

Insufficient ablation analysis: Gaussian lifetime initialized to arbitrary '4x frame time' without justification or sensitivity analysis; alpha loss weight (0.1), learning rate reduction (10^-2), and Tikhonov parameter τ₀ not ablated; voxel size impact not discussed despite being initialization parameter

Small synthetic evaluation dataset: Only 3 scenes with 150 total velocity fields; no statistical significance testing; DVE protocol validated only on simpler synthetic scenes rather than real flames where motion is more turbulent

Methodological gaps: Circular dependency between flow projection (relying on depth) and depth optimization (using flow) not analyzed for stability; background removal via minimum intensity projection only valid for static camera with fire-only motion; motion mask M generation not detailed

Limited scope and generalization: Highly specialized to controlled fire reconstruction with unclear extension to other transient phenomena; no handling of smoke; method unlikely to inspire general techniques for dynamic reconstruction; impact limited to narrow fire/flame reconstruction community

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear analysis of why existing GS methods fail (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift)
Practical hardware contribution: clever ESP32-based synchronization achieving microsecond precision using rolling shutter effects
Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation combining multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, depth) with novel density-weighted volumetric evaluation (DVE) protocol for motion assessment
Thorough ablation studies (6 variants) with clear demonstration of component importance and complementary metrics
Clear quantitative and qualitative superiority over baselines across real-world and synthetic scenarios
Excellent documentation and reproducibility effort with detailed supplementary material, per-scene results, and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: combines existing techniques (optical flow initialization, static/dynamic decomposition, velocity parameterization from FreeTimeGS) without significant innovation

Extremely narrow scope: only evaluated on fire with specific 3-camera synchronized hardware setup; unclear if applicable to other transient/emissive phenomena despite motivation suggesting broader use

Overly heavy regularization masking core underconstrained problem: 100× amplification of depth loss weight and reliance on external monocular depth priors (DepthAnythingV2) bias solutions rather than principled geometry handling

Inadequate motion model: constant linear velocity is acknowledged as insufficient for turbulent flames; 4-frame lifetime appears arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis or ground-truth motion comparison on real scenes
Synchronization ablation undermines claimed importance: NoSync shows negligible PSNR drop (26.93→26.89) and improved motion metrics, suggesting custom hardware may not be critical

DVE evaluation metric only validated on 3 synthetic Mantaflow scenes; assumes Gaussian distribution for fire (questionable), uses unquantified approximations, and only applicable where ground-truth velocity fields exist

Reproducibility concerns: uses unofficial FreeTimeGS implementation (OpsiClear/FreeTimeGsVanilla) rather than author-provided code; motion mask creation method unclear; fire removal via minimum intensity projection is heuristic

Limited practical applicability: small real-world dataset (17 videos, ~68 seconds total from single setup), requires controlled environment, perfect camera calibration, and specialized hardware; no real-world applications discussed

Trade-off between appearance and physical accuracy inadequately addressed: NoMask ablation shows PSNR improvements when motion mask removed, suggesting optimization for visual fidelity rather than true reconstruction

Missing critical comparisons and analyses: no comparison to tomographic or physics-informed methods; no evaluation on other dynamic/emissive phenomena; missing sensitivity analyses for camera count, calibration errors, and frame rate requirements

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of three specific failure modes (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift) in existing GS methods when applied to fire reconstruction
Thoughtful system design appropriately decomposing static/dynamic components with flow-based initialization of transient Gaussians carrying explicit lifetime and velocity parameters

Comprehensive experimental validation including 17 diverse real-world fire sequences at 400 Hz, 3 synthetic scenes with ground truth velocity fields, and thorough ablations clearly isolating each component's contribution
Novel DVE (density-weighted volumetric evaluation) metric addresses circular dependency problem in motion field evaluation and provides both magnitude and directional motion accuracy measures
Practical hardware engineering demonstrating 15 µs sub-frame temporal synchronization using LED-based rolling shutter exploitation, showing commitment to reproducibility
Consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple metrics (PSNRflame: 26.93 vs 24.48 second-best; CosSim: 0.744 vs 0.225 baseline; RMSEdepth: 0.094 vs 0.113 second-best)
Honest discussion of limitations (optical flow dependency, linear velocity model inadequacy, background-foreground separation assumptions) without overstating generalizability
Clear presentation with effective visualizations demonstrating method advantages and baseline failure modes
weaknesses: Narrow application scope limited to fire reconstruction with unclear transferability to other transient volumetric phenomena (smoke, explosions, water spray), constraining broader impact

Critical unmitigated dependency on optical flow quality: entire dynamic Gaussian initialization relies on accurate dense flow, but only single RandFlow ablation provided; robustness to flow estimation failure in low-texture or semi-transparent flame regions not investigated

Linear velocity model fundamentally mismatches real flame dynamics exhibiting turbulent acceleration and complex motion; acknowledged limitation offers no solution, risking temporal blurring and coherence degradation over longer sequences

Unresolved trade-off between visual fidelity and physical plausibility: NoMask ablation reveals alpha loss improves motion accuracy (+2% CosSim) but reduces visual quality (-2.5% SSIM full frame, -3.3% flame region); no principled solution for application-dependent weighting provided

Custom ESP32 hardware synchronization significantly limits accessibility and reproducibility; NoSync ablation shows timing is consequential, making the method impractical without specialized hardware investment

Limited technical novelty in individual components: stereo+monocular depth fusion is standard practice, 3D flow back-projection via multi-view constraints is straightforward geometry, constant velocity model borrowed from FreeTimeGS; novelty primarily in system combination rather than fundamental techniques

Insufficient analysis of background-foreground interaction assumptions: method assumes minimal coupling, but no failure cases demonstrated for large-scale fires, smoke-rich scenes, or ember-on-background scenarios despite dataset being limited to 17 controlled small-to-medium fires
Incomplete failure mode analysis: no investigation of which flame patterns (highly vortical, rapidly accelerating, semi-transparent) cause degradation, or error stratification by scene properties

Baseline comparison confound: FreeTimeGS uses different initialization (RoMa) than other methods (COLMAP) due to unofficial implementation; re-implementation with standard initialization would strengthen comparison
Small synthetic evaluation set (3 scenes only) at 640³ resolution; lacks systematic parameter sweeps examining sensitivity to flame intensity, motion speed, turbulence, and initialization quality
